query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Inducing nanoscale Cu-rich precipitation within the FeNiCrCoCu high‐entropy alloy coating enhances wear resistance during high-temperature sliding by increasing load sharing and pinning dislocations, thereby reducing microscopic plastic deformation.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited FeNiCrCoCu coating with a largely homogeneous solid solution lacking significant nanoscale phase separation.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled post-deposition thermal treatment designed to promote the formation and refinement of Cu-rich precipitates (e.g., heating at an optimized temperature/time that is high enough to drive Cu segregation without degrading the overall coating integrity).
generation.conditions: High-temperature sliding regime, approximately 600–700 °C, under controlled normal loads on a conventional metal substrate.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale Cu-rich precipitates, possibly located along grain boundaries and/or dispersed within the coarse matrix.
generation.mechanism: The formation of fine, dispersive Cu-rich precipitates provides an additional strengthening mechanism through Orowan-type dislocation pinning and load-transfer effects. These precipitates impede dislocation motion and limit localized plastic deformation during high-temperature sliding, thus enhancing overall wear resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline homogeneous coating, the thermally treated coating exhibiting Cu-rich precipitates will show reduced wear volume and shallower wear scars, accompanied by lower densities of mobile dislocations upon microscopic analysis.
generation.baseline: The as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu coating without intentional thermal treatment, where the microstructure remains homogeneous.
generation.boundary: The predicted benefits are expected to hold under high-temperature sliding conditions (600–700 °C) and moderate contact stresses. At significantly higher temperatures or under severe oxidative environments, the mechanism may be obscured by other high-temperature phenomena (e.g., enhanced oxidation or creep).
generation.uncertainty: The precise volume fraction, size, and spatial distribution of the Cu-rich precipitates required to optimize wear resistance is not yet quantified, and competing high-temperature processes (such as oxidation) might influence the outcome.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of FeNiCrCoCu coatings on an identical conventional metal substrate. One group (control) remains in the as-deposited state, while the second group is subjected to a controlled thermal treatment intended to promote nanoscale Cu-rich precipitation. Subject both groups to identical high-temperature sliding wear tests at ~650 °C under the same load and sliding speed. Post-test, analyze the wear scars (using profilometry or 3D surface scans) and perform microscopic (TEM or SEM) and compositional (EDS) analyses to evaluate precipitate formation and dislocation structures.
measurements: Wear volume or scar depth using profilometry
Dislocation density and plastic deformation features via TEM
Presence, size, and distribution of Cu-rich precipitates via high-resolution SEM/TEM with EDS
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermally-treated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in wear volume/scar depth and show no evidence of Cu-rich precipitate formation or related dislocation pinning compared to the as-deposited control, then the hypothesis that Cu-rich precipitation governs improved wear resistance and reduced microscopic deformation is falsified.

Question: How can high-throughput computational screening be used to discover lightweight, precipitation-strengthened high-entropy alloys with high-temperature strength superior to traditional ferritic superalloys?. System: Al–Cr–Fe–Mn–Ti quinary system (specifically Al20Cr5Fe50Mn20Ti5 and Al15Cr5Fe50Mn25Ti5 as successful cases). Processing: Arc-melting of 99.9 wt% purity constituent elements, melted at least six times for homogeneity, followed by drop-casting; subsequent homogenization at 1200 °C and annealing at 700 °C for 2 hours for specific characterizations. Test conditions: Compression tests at room temperature and elevated temperatures (up to 700 °C) at a strain rate of 2 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹; in situ neutron scattering from room temperature to 1050 °C; synchrotron XRD and TEM characterization.
